title: The green revolution is unstoppable: Adam Tooze on “the single most dramatic story in the history of energy”
gist: Adam Tooze argues the Hormuz closure, the 14th fossil-fuel shock since the 1970s, reinforces an unstoppable green-energy transition powered by cheap Chinese electrotech, whose success stems from credible top-level commitment rather than novel policy tools. He faults Europe's carmakers and power-market design for its political backlash, urges an EU-China car bargain, sees off-grid solar transforming African development, and flags pandemics as the most neglected macro risk.

insights.claim: The Strait of Hormuz closure was, in physical terms, the largest interruption to the global energy system ever, yet its impact on wealthy, energy-secure economies was milder than predicted.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Rich importers with purchasing power absorbed the shock; the pain is concentrated elsewhere, limiting DM macro damage.
insights.quote: This is, after all, in physical terms, the largest interruption to the global energy system ever, essentially.
insights.locator: Well, we've really learned about asymmetry

insights.claim: The Hormuz shock hit lower-income energy importers such as Thailand, India, Pakistan and Bangladesh hardest, revealing a sharp asymmetry by purchasing power.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: EM importers lower in the purchasing-power pecking order face outsized balance-of-payments and inflation stress from energy shocks.
insights.quote: Except not if you're in Thailand or not if you're in India or Pakistan or Bangladesh
insights.locator: Well, we've really learned about asymmetry

insights.claim: The fertiliser-price shock from the Gulf disruption has yet to hit low-income farmers; its consequences will show up in the next cropping cycle rather than immediately.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Lagged food-security and food-inflation risk in poorer countries is a second-order effect still to come.
insights.quote: not now immediately but in the next cropping cycle
insights.locator: Well, we've really learned about asymmetry

insights.claim: Oil prices did not spike to the $150-200 per barrel many predicted during the crisis; the lasting impact comes from forcing governments and households to question supply security itself.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Policy response (diversification, electrification) is driven by perceived insecurity, not just realized prices.
insights.quote: Many people would have been predicting $150, $200 a barrel. That's not happened.
insights.locator: Yes, we're moving in a different direction

insights.claim: Citing Javier Blas of Bloomberg, this is the 14th major shock to the fossil fuel system since the early 1970s, profoundly discrediting oil and gas as a reliable power source.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Repeated shocks strengthen the structural case for energy diversification away from imported hydrocarbons.
insights.quote: this is the 14th major shock to the fossil fuel system since the early 1970s
insights.locator: I mean, I think the simple story

insights.claim: The 1973-79 oil shocks were an inflection point where developed-world fossil fuel consumption and CO2 emission curves broke; the US later eased back up while Europe kept declining.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Historical precedent suggests the current shock could similarly bend demand curves, especially in import-dependent Europe.
insights.quote: the the 73-79 shocks are an inflection point
insights.locator: Yes, we're moving in a different direction

insights.claim: Countries will diversify away from oil and gas; US LNG exports benefited Europe and softened its shock, but the more optimistic outcome is a surge in imports of Chinese green electrotech (solar, batteries, EVs).
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Bullish demand signal for Chinese solar, battery and EV exporters and for US LNG in the near term.
insights.quote: we're going to see a surge in imports of Chinese green technology, of green electrotech
insights.locator: I mean, I think the simple story

themes.theme: Chinese green-tech dependence vs oil dependence

insights.claim: China's dominance of green electrical technology is more monopolistic than OPEC's position in oil and gas, which is why countries hesitate to rely on it.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Supply-chain concentration risk in clean-energy hardware is a key policy and trade-barrier driver.
insights.quote: China's dominance of green electrical technology is far more clear than, for instance, that of OPEC over oil and gas
insights.locator: Well, because they are basically making

insights.claim: Buying green hardware is structurally a different bargain from importing fossil fuels: once installed and operating, there is no ongoing import dependence, unlike recurring oil and gas purchases.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Energy security calculus favors one-off capex dependence over flow dependence on fuel imports.
insights.quote: once you bought the kit, as long as you can keep it operating, you've got no further dependence
insights.locator: Well, because they are basically making

insights.claim: Concerns about potential kill switches in Chinese PV inverters and tracking devices in BYD cars are unaddressed; Beijing is missing an opportunity to run a test-and-verify global energy-security forum.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Security verification mechanisms could unlock wider adoption of Chinese green tech; absence keeps trade frictions elevated.
insights.quote: you need some sort of test and verify kind of mechanism I think to address this concern
insights.locator: Well, because they are basically making

insights.claim: Full energy autonomy is an illusion; the real task is choosing, managing, hedging and diversifying risks.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Frames energy policy as portfolio risk management rather than self-sufficiency.
insights.quote: radical independence, full autonomy in the modern world is an illusion in any case
insights.locator: Well, because they are basically making

insights.claim: Europe's reluctance to rely on Chinese green tech stems largely from China's alignment with Russia in the Ukraine war, yet Europe still imported tens of gigawatts of Chinese PV after a 2022 spike.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Geopolitics caps but does not stop European purchases of Chinese solar.
insights.quote: Tens of gigawatts of photovoltaics were imported. That continues.
insights.locator: Well, because they are basically making

insights.claim: Europe's condition for Chinese EV entry is effectively minimum prices, making European consumers overpay to protect an auto supply chain employing over 12 million people.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: EU price undertakings/tariffs protect incumbents at consumers' expense; job protection is the binding political constraint.
insights.quote: the motor vehicle industry is a huge established industry with over 12 million employees in Europe in the broader supply chain
insights.locator: They're literally going to insist

insights.claim: A EU-China car trade war is avoidable; if it happens it will reflect lack of political will, since the stakes are transparent and deals via Chinese FDI conditions are already being discussed.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Expect negotiated outcomes (local production via Chinese FDI) rather than outright trade war as the base case the author favors.
insights.quote: if they manage to make this into a trade war right now, it's for a lack of political will
insights.locator: They're literally going to insist

insights.claim: Unlike the US, where Biden imposed 100% tariffs on Chinese EVs and asked Canada and Mexico to follow, Europe has no fundamental objection to Chinese cars, which are arriving anyway.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Chinese automakers' European market share growth looks more durable than in North America.
insights.quote: even Joe Biden put 100% tariff on Chinese EVs and then asked Canada and Mexico to do the same
insights.locator: They're literally going to insist

insights.claim: European carmakers failed to prepare for decarbonisation despite it being in EU plans 15 years ago, instead perfecting the turbo diesel, and owners (largely private in Germany) extracted tens of billions in dividends that should have funded next-generation technology.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Underinvestment explains European auto weakness vs Chinese EV makers and forces costly political compromises.
insights.quote: they took tens of billions of euros in dividends, which should have been ploughed back into the next generation of technology
insights.locator: Well, it's one of the biggest challenges

insights.claim: China's emissions surge from 2000 and plateau since the mid-2010s, now a genuine plateau, is the most dramatic story in the history of energy and industrialisation, driven by COVID, deliberate construction slowdown and Xi's dual-carbon pledge (peak, then net zero by 2060).
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Chinese emissions plateau undercuts the case that global emissions can't peak and reshapes coal/commodity demand outlooks.
insights.quote: It's the single most dramatic story in the history of energy or industrialism or the economy in history.
insights.locator: Yes, it's the single most dramatic

insights.claim: China's experience negates the idea that government policy is dead as a driver of the global economy.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Industrial policy can reshape global industries; investors should price state direction seriously.
insights.quote: The idea that, you know, government policy is dead as a driver of the global economy, it's all completely negated by this Chinese experience
insights.locator: Yes, it's the single most dramatic

insights.claim: China's policy tools (industrial subsidies, demand stimulus, fixed prices, feed-in tariffs, near carbon pricing, clean-air regulation) are standard and largely borrowed from Europe; the difference is credible, top-level political commitment, with climate ranking fourth in five-year-plan communication.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Credibility and consistency of commitment, not novel instruments, determine transition speed.
insights.quote: The difference to everywhere else in the world is not at the level of the policy instruments
insights.locator: Yes, it's the single most dramatic

insights.claim: Best Western estimates put total Chinese subsidy for the EV industry at about $150 billion over 15 years, roughly $10 billion a year, not out of line with what other societies contemplate.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: The scale of subsidy was modest; consistency and entrepreneurial response mattered more than size.
insights.quote: Best Western estimates of the total subsidy for the EV industry, which is a world-changing event, are in the order of $150 billion over 15 years.
insights.locator: Yes, it's the single most dramatic

insights.claim: Chinese firms in photovoltaics, batteries and EVs are barely profitable but compete fiercely, motivated by the prospect of becoming a national champion rather than near-term returns.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Persistent overcapacity and thin margins in Chinese clean-tech; deflationary pressure on global green hardware prices.
insights.quote: people aren't making a lot of money right now in photovoltaics or batteries or EVs in China
insights.locator: Yes, it's the single most dramatic

insights.claim: Domestic air pollution, as in Dalian or Tianjin a decade ago, was a key driver of China's clean strategy alongside global climate concerns.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Local co-benefits sustain policy commitment independent of climate diplomacy.
insights.locator: Yes, it's the single most dramatic

themes.theme: Western political failure on climate and power pricing

insights.claim: A one-party Marxist-Leninist state may prove more able to consistently follow science-based policy than Western democracies, a sobering prospect the world is on the cusp of.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Policy volatility in democracies raises risk premia on Western green investment relative to China.
insights.quote: finds it easier to consistently cleave to a science-based policy than policy in the West
insights.locator: Well, it's one of the biggest challenges

insights.claim: Climate-sceptic populist parties such as Reform UK (threatening to undo offshore wind contracts) and Germany's AfD represent a failure of rationality in Western democracy.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Political risk to UK offshore wind CfDs and German green policy if these parties gain power.
insights.quote: Reform has threatened to undo long-term contracts for offshore wind farms
insights.locator: Well, it's one of the biggest challenges

insights.claim: Europe linked the green transition to high energy prices because marginal gas and coal plants set prices in unbundled electricity markets, even though wind and solar are near free or negative-priced on good days; China does the opposite, driving power prices down and supply up.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Market-design reform (decoupling from marginal gas pricing) is key to political durability of Europe's transition.
insights.quote: But the marginal price, which is what governs the price in a de-unbundled electricity market, is being set by the polluting gas and coal-fired power stations.
insights.locator: Well, this is what we see in Texas

insights.claim: A rational European strategy needs three consistent instruments: low consumer electricity prices, major incentives to shift generation to green, and carbon penalties on dirty generation.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Watch for policy moves toward cheap electricity plus carbon penalties as a signal of European strategic correction.
insights.quote: You need three instruments effectively to be working and to be working consistently.
insights.locator: Well, this is what we see in Texas

insights.claim: Europe's failure stemmed from overconfidence in carbon pricing without thinking through marginal-gas price setting, austerity-minded energy up-pricing to induce efficiency, and until five or six years ago an allergy to directly supporting manufacturers.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Explains lagging European clean-tech manufacturing; Green Deal and Next Gen EU are partial corrections disrupted by the Ukraine war.
insights.quote: there was too much confidence, I think, over optimistic belief in the logic of carbon pricing per se
insights.locator: Well, there was too much confidence

themes.theme: Development, flying geese and off-grid Africa

insights.claim: Fears that automation and cheap power will stop manufacturing migrating out of China are overstated; Bangladesh in textiles and Vietnam, which built its own industrial clusters and retained Chinese green tech for decarbonisation, are counter-examples.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: The flying-geese dispersion to South and Southeast Asia continues, supporting those manufacturing bases.
insights.quote: There's mixed evidence on this.
insights.locator: There's mixed evidence on this.

insights.claim: China did not kill African industrialisation; it was halted by the 1970s oil shocks, subsequent IMF programmes and the HIV crisis.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Reframes China's role in Africa as enabler of new development paths rather than competitor.
insights.quote: China didn't kill the prospects of industrialization in Africa.
insights.locator: There's mixed evidence on this.

insights.claim: African Development Bank and World Bank programmes aim to electrify about 300 million people in Africa for a couple of tens of billions of dollars using cheap solar, batteries and inverters, opening off-grid development paths where grids like Nigeria's do not exist.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Large distributed-solar demand pool in Africa for cheap Chinese hardware; leapfrogging grid build-out.
insights.quote: electrify the homes of about 300 million people in Africa
insights.locator: What China offers for the first time

insights.claim: Pandemics are an under-discussed macro risk: COVID was mild yet cut output about 20% in three to four months, a hit beyond even the worst climate models, and a serious Ebola outbreak in Africa is getting little attention.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Tail-risk portfolios underweight pandemic shocks relative to their potential severity.
insights.quote: That is off the charts of even the worst climate models.
insights.locator: 20% down in the space of three months

insights.claim: Unfilled WHO budget gaps have left the organisation essentially unable to handle the Ebola crisis, which should be top priority.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Underfunded global health surveillance raises odds of an uncontained outbreak.
insights.quote: more people didn't immediately set up to fill in the WHO budget
insights.locator: 20% down in the space of three months

insights.claim: Unlike El Nino-type climate events, pandemic timing cannot be forecast, which contributes to collective under-preparation despite high odds of one over the next decade.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Unforecastable timing leads markets and policymakers to discount the risk.
insights.quote: I can't even forecast it like an El Niño event.
insights.locator: 20% down in the space of three months

themes.theme: Geopolitics: Iran war and China as anchor

insights.claim: The US-Israeli attack on Iran shows the world no longer fits Davos's premise of good-will actors pursuing common prosperity, creating cognitive dissonance at such forums.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Geopolitical violence undermines stability-for-growth assumptions underpinning global investment.
insights.quote: the American and Israeli attack on Iran demonstrates that that's just not the world that we are in
insights.locator: I mean it's a difficult issue

insights.claim: With Europe lining up behind the US and Israel, China is left as the one big anchor of stability in the world, pursuing its interests in a stable, predictable, prosperity-oriented way.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Supports the case for engagement with China as a relatively predictable counterpart.
insights.quote: you're left essentially with China as the one big anchor of stability in the world
insights.locator: Not publicly, certainly
